say.text: A 45-year-old woman has an operable 2.5 cm carcinoma of the breast. Her axilla feels clinically normal.
Which is the current standard operation for her?

choices.label: Halsted radical mastectomy with full axillary clearance
Simple mastectomy with no axillary staging at all
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Compare what each option removes. Then ask what the patient still needs after the operation to make the treatment complete.
Right. Breast conservation with whole-breast radiotherapy gives survival equivalent to mastectomy in suitable early cancers.
Whole-breast radiotherapy is mandatory after conservation. When conservation is not suitable, modified radical mastectomy is the alternative.
That choice is not right.
Halsted takes pectoralis major and minor and all three axillary levels, and it is now rarely done.
It looks the most thorough, and older keys did expect it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: old keys still teach Halsted as the standard, and that is the model to replace.

say.text: That is not right. Removing the breast alone looks like a clean, simple plan, and it tempts when you want to skip the axilla decision.
But early cancer needs surgery to both the breast and the axilla, and the axilla still needs staging.
Breast-conserving surgery with whole-breast radiotherapy is the current standard when the tumour can be cleared with clear margins and the breast suits conservation.
Halsted, which removes pectoralis major and minor, is no longer the standard.
MRM keeps pectoralis major and is used when conservation is unsuitable, for example with multicentric disease.
A 42-year-old is being considered for breast-conserving surgery.
Which of these rules it out?

choices.label: Positive lymph nodes in the axilla
A tumour larger than 5 cm in size
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what conservation needs: clear margins from one excision, and a breast that can take whole-breast radiotherapy. Which option threatens that?
Right. Disease in separate quadrants cannot be cleared through one excision, so conservation is ruled out.
That is not right. Size looks like a hard limit, and a 5 cm line is easy to carry over from staging.
But size matters only relative to the breast, as a cosmetic problem, not as an absolute bar.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: size is weighed against the breast, not treated as a fixed bar.

say.text: That is not right. Positive nodes feel like a bad sign, so they seem to close the breast option too.
But node status governs the axilla, not whether the breast can be kept.
Multicentric disease, or diffuse malignant-appearing microcalcifications, is a contraindication to conservation.
So are previous breast or chest-wall radiotherapy, pregnancy needing radiotherapy, persistently positive margins and inflammatory carcinoma.
A 50-year-old has a 2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. Her axilla is clinically node-negative.
What is the first axillary procedure?

choices.label: Sentinel lymph node biopsy, to find out if the nodes hold cancer
Level I and II axillary dissection, to remove any nodal cancer
No axillary procedure, as the nodes feel normal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the surgeon needs to learn from the axilla first, and what a full clearance is for in a patient whose nodes feel normal.
Right. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is the standard axillary staging for clinically node-negative invasive cancer.
Dissection is for a positive axilla, and after one or two positive sentinel nodes it can be omitted when the breast is conserved and radiotherapy is given.
That is not right. Clearing the axilla feels thorough, and it was how older practice handled the armpit first.
But routine dissection carries morbidity such as lymphoedema and shoulder stiffness, so it is reserved for a node-positive axilla.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: older practice cleared the axilla first, but staging by sentinel biopsy now comes first.

say.text: That is not right. Node-negative can sound like no test is needed, so skipping the axilla looks reasonable.
But the axilla still has to be staged before the plan is final, because nodal status changes the treatment.
Clinically node-negative invasive cancer is staged by sentinel lymph node biopsy, using radioisotope and/or blue dye.
Dissection is not the first step. It is for a node-positive axilla, where sentinel biopsy is not the staging route.
Since the Z0011 trial, one or two positive sentinel nodes treated with conservation and whole-breast radiotherapy allow ALND to be omitted.
A patient has an axillary clearance for node-positive disease.
Which nerve is most often injured in this dissection?

choices.label: The long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior
The thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi
The intercostobrachial nerve in the axilla
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Separate the nerve that is injured most often from the one that causes the most striking deficit. Which deficit does a patient report most after clearance?
Right. Intercostobrachial nerve injury is the commonest, giving numbness of the medial upper arm and axilla.
Winging of the scapula comes from the long thoracic nerve, which is the more dramatic but less common deficit.
Together: conserve when suitable, use MRM when not, stage a node-negative axilla with SLNB, and match each nerve to its deficit.
That is not right. Winging of the scapula is the deficit most people remember, so it is tempting to count the nerve that causes it.
But dramatic is not the same as frequent. Winging comes from the long thoracic nerve, a less common injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: dramatic winging does not mean the nerve behind it is the commonest injury.

say.text: That is not right. Thoracodorsal injury is a real deficit of axillary surgery, and it is easy to recall from the anatomy.
But it only weakens latissimus dorsi, a power problem in the arm, and it is not the commonest axillary nerve injury.
The intercostobrachial nerve is the commonest injury, and its loss gives numbness of the medial upper arm.
Long thoracic injury paralyses serratus anterior and causes winging of the scapula.
Thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi.
Let us test that again from another angle. A woman with operable cancer is not suitable for breast conservation.
Which operation should the plan name?

choices.label: Simple mastectomy, leaving the armpit for later
Halsted radical mastectomy, the definitive operation here
Modified radical mastectomy, preserving pectoralis major
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The operation here is modified radical mastectomy. It removes the breast and the axillary nodes and keeps pectoralis major.
Yes. Modified radical mastectomy removes the breast and the axillary nodes and keeps pectoralis major, so it is the alternative when conservation is unsuitable.
Not right. Deferring the armpit feels like a cautious shortcut when the breast is being removed anyway.
An operable cancer still needs the axilla dealt with at the same operation, so deferring it is not a safe plan.
Not right. The definitive label from older keys makes the most extensive operation feel like the safe answer.
Halsted removed pectoralis major and minor along with all three axillary levels, and is now rarely done.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the most extensive operation is not today's default.

say.text: Step 1 is the wrong one. A 6 cm tumour is a relative issue against breast size and cosmesis, not an absolute bar, so the step overstates the size rule.
Yes. Size is judged against the breast and against cosmesis, so a 6 cm tumour is a relative problem, not an absolute bar to conservation.
Let us test that again from another angle. A woman has a 6 cm tumour in a moderate-sized breast. Chemotherapy shrinks it to 2 cm. A classmate's three-step plan has one wrong step.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 2: conservation is possible once it has shrunk to 2 cm
Step 1: a 6 cm tumour rules out conservation on size alone
Step 3: whole-breast radiotherapy after any conservation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a 5 cm figure measures: the tumour alone, or the tumour against the breast it sits in.
Not right. Radiotherapy feels like the step to drop once the breast has been cut, so it looks like the weak point.
Whole-breast radiotherapy is mandatory after conservation, so this step is the standard one.
Not right. Shrinkage to 2 cm looks like a loophole around a fixed size rule, so step 2 feels like the one to challenge.
But step 2 is sound: chemotherapy can downstage a tumour to allow conservation. The wrong step is step 1, which treats 6 cm as an absolute bar.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at the size rule: a fixed limit is not the test here.

say.text: Let us test that again from another angle. Now the reason. Why is clearing the armpit first the wrong order for this woman?

choices.label: It dissects an armpit that only needed staging
It is the classical first step, with biopsy only as a fallback
It risks lymphoedema, a real but secondary cost

say.text: Not right. Clearance is the old key's first step, so it feels like the safe default.
Old keys cleared the armpit before knowing its status. For a clinically node-negative axilla, sentinel node biopsy is the standard staging.
The step is wrong because it dissects an armpit that only needed staging. Sentinel node biopsy stages a clinically node-negative armpit, and dissection follows only if the node is positive.
Not right. Lymphoedema is a worry after clearance, so the step feels risky, and that makes it tempting.
Lymphoedema is a real complication of axillary dissection, but it is a cost of the step, not the reason the order is wrong.
Yes. Staging a node-negative armpit needs only the sentinel node, so a full clearance adds morbidity without answering a new question.
Not right. Winging is the most dramatic deficit, so the nerve behind it feels like the most common one.
Frequency and drama are different questions. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed, and its injury gives numbness of the medial arm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate frequency from drama: they are different questions.

say.text: Separate two questions: which nerve is injured most often, and which deficit is the most striking.
Let us test that again from another angle. A classmate is counselling a woman after an axillary clearance. One of these three statements is wrong.
Which statement?

choices.label: The long thoracic nerve is the commonest nerve injured
The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed
Long thoracic injury causes winging of the scapula
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The wrong statement is the one calling the long thoracic nerve the commonest. It gives the striking winging, but the intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed.
Yes. The long thoracic nerve causes the dramatic winging, but it is not the commonest injury. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed.
Not right. Winging is a vivid deficit, so a statement about it feels like the place to look for an error.
Long thoracic injury paralyses serratus anterior and makes the scapula wing. That statement is textbook.
Size is different. A large tumour is only a relative issue, for cosmesis, not an absolute bar.
Connective tissue disease raises radiation toxicity.
Ask which operation removes the breast and the axillary nodes but keeps the chest muscle.
